user.cardiac_stress_test_summary_plain_englis: Plain-English refresher: A cardiac stress test checks how your heart performs under activity. It helps diagnose coronary artery disease, assess risk, or guide treatment. How it goes: you exercise on a treadmill or pedal a bike while heart rate, blood pressure, and ECG are monitored; imaging or scans may follow to look at heart motion or blood flow. Types include: treadmill/bike with ECG, treadmill with imaging, pharmacologic stress tests if you can't exercise (drugs to mimic exercise). Prep: avoid caffeine for 12-24 hours, wear comfy clothing/shoes, bring meds list, follow doctor instructions about meals or meds, arrange transport if needed. During: you may feel short of breath, chest discomfort, or dizziness; signals to stop are chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or dizziness. After: you rest; results may be immediate or take a few days; some tests use low-dose radiation. Risks are low; your doctor will explain benefits and risks. Talking with clinician: ask what the results mean, what next steps are, and whether any meds need adjustment.

user.email_agent_mvp_plan: Idea: Build an autonomous-email agent with its own alias/address that can read inbox, draft replies, and present them for user approval before sending. MVP plan: 1) Create a dedicated mailbox (agent@domain) with hosting/domain and secure access. 2) Use IMAP/SMTP or provider APIs for reading and sending; AI drafts via OpenAI or similar. 3) Implement a guardrail: human-in-the-loop for sending; content filters; disclaimers that it’s an assistant. 4) Memory to store user preferences (tone, safe topics, typical responses). 5) Simple UI (CLI or small web UI) to review drafts, edit, and approve. 6) Logging/audit trail of drafts vs sent messages and approvals. 7) Security considerations: OAuth2 or app-specific passwords, encryption at rest in a local vault, minimal data retention. 8) Milestones: MVP draft (read-only drafts), then send after approval, then memory and tone control, then guardrails and testing.
